item.title: Wine 11.23 fixes some gaming bugs, boosts DirectX 12 compatibility, and adds Arm64 macOS support
item.itunes:title: Wine 11.23 fixes some gaming bugs, boosts DirectX 12 compatibility, and adds Arm64 macOS support
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Wine 11.23 adds Arm64 macOS support, enabling easier Windows apps on Apple Silicon.
  • VKD3D upgraded to 2.2 to boost Direct3D 12 compatibility and game performance.
  • It also includes fixes for games like Mafia III, RollerCoaster Tycoon, Arknights and The Sims.

While compatibility with Linux games has only improved as the years go on thanks to Proton, sometimes you still need to reach for the trusty, not-an-emulator superstar Wine.

The newest version, Wine 11.23, fixes some annoying bugs when playing specific games and helps boost Direct3D 12 compatibility. However, those using macOS on Arm64 will be more excited about this update's main highlight.

Wine 11.23 adds Arm64 macOS compatibility into the mix

Plus, a slew of bug fixes and Direct3D 12 tweaks

As announced on the Wine GitLab website (via Linuxiac), version 11.23 is ready for people to grab. The big new feature brings Wine to macOS running on Arm64 architecture, which is a good reminder that Wine isn't just for Linux users. By bringing Wine to the Arm64 macOS scene, people can get Windows apps running on their Apple machines more easily than ever.

For everyone else, the update still has some nice tweaks. VKD3D, which helps translate Direct3D 12 calls into Vulkan, has been upgraded to version 2.2 to improve DirectX 12 game compatibility and performance

Plus, there are some nice bug fixes for a handful of games, including these highlights:

RollerCoaster Tycoon 1 and 2: some icons appear black in Load/Save Game dialogs

Mafia III: Definitive Edition doesn't get past intro

Star Trek: Elite Force II: corrupted screen with anti-aliasing and EmulateModeset=Y

Arknights: Endfield crashes on unimplemented function ntoskrnl.exe.PsGetProcessImageFileName

SafeDisc driver for The Sims 1 (all versions) failed to create driver "\Registry\Machine\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\Secdrv"

To grab it, head over to the Wine download page, or wait for the update to roll out to your distro or Flatpak.

Wine 11 rewrites how Linux runs Windows games at the kernel level, and the speed gains are massive

Wine 11 is the biggest jump for Linux gaming in years.

38
By  Adam Conway

item.title: I don't miss hunting for drivers on Windows because Linux just works out of the box
item.itunes:title: I don't miss hunting for drivers on Windows because Linux just works out of the box
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One of the biggest reasons I see people give for not moving from Windows to Linux is that the latter has a reputation for being hard to set up. And they're not entirely wrong; there are some new things you need to learn and adapt to, especially if you pick an advanced distro. I'm not going to pretend that using Windows is as difficult as booting up an Arch Linux ISO and hand-crafting your OS line by line.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

At the same time, there are some areas of Linux I think are a lot easier than Windows. For instance, despite Linux long being the OS where hardware didn't play nicely with it, I think about compatibility issues a lot less with it than I ever did with Windows.

Windows has the big driver hunt attached to it

I don't miss downloading drivers at all

When I used Windows, I thought fighting with drivers was part of every OS. Now, I am a huge Linux fanboy, but I'll rein in my criticisms of Windows instead of going all-in against it. Because, let's face it, if you bought a piece of hardware off Amazon, it's going to have drivers for Windows. Compatibility was never an issue. Installing the drivers was usually fine, too. Usually.

But there were always moments when it wasn't fine, and those were the most annoying. For instance, a company may keep its drivers updated to a certain point and stop, meaning they'd break after a Windows update. Sometimes Windows itself would decide to install a driver for you, and it would mess things up. And having to reinstall drivers when things went wrong was always a pain.

Running Windows apps on Linux just changed forever, and I was one of the first to try it

Things are diferent now

34
By  João Carrasqueira

Linux puts most of the drivers into the kernel itself

No hunting around for downloads

Linux, on the other hand, does things a little differently. If you're unsure as to how Linux works, every distro uses the Linux kernel as its core. It's the beating heart that all Linux distros share, even if some perform bleeding-edge kernel updates while others perform them at a glacial speed.

When the Linux community needs to get hardware running on Linux, they make a driver within the kernel. It's usually a handful of people opting to get a specific device working on Linux and adding code to the kernel that properly recognizes and uses the hardware. Once the kernel maintainers review the code and give it the thumbs-up, it gets bundled into the next kernel version. That kernel then gets distributed as an update to all the distros that accept new kernel updates. Now, all the distros that keep their kernel current support that hardware. Easy peasy.

Case in point: I recently purchased a TP-Link USB Bluetooth adapter for my Linux PC. Unfortunately, the device was so recent that it didn't come with Linux support. However, the good news was that the community added compatibility for it in the next Linux update, and that update was in the Release Candidate phase. Think of it like a public beta test for a kernel before it's released into the wild.

So, I downloaded the Release Candidate build, got my Bluetooth dongle working, and helped test it out as a daily driver. Fortunately, the people who developed the drivers were very skilled, as I didn't have to report a single bug. It eventually arrived on the release version of the kernel, and now every Linux distro that supports the newest kernel version supports my Bluetooth dongle.

Plus, as long as the community wants to keep supporting the hardware, the driver will keep receiving patches long into the future. There's no risk of the manufacturer deeming your dongle too old to make patches for; in fact, the Linux kernel still supports some really old hardware.

I'd pick a 10-year-old desktop running Linux over a new $300 Windows laptop every time

It's not even close, honestly.

13
By  Simon Batt

As useful as it is, it's not perfect

It does have its flaws

As much as I'd love to herald Linux's way of handling drivers as the best way to go about things, it does have problems. For one, device compatibility is sometimes based on the whim of the community. If nobody wants to make it compatible with Linux, it likely won't ever get full support. Meanwhile, if a manufacturer releases hardware for Windows, the onus is on it to release drivers for it, meaning drivers are available on day one.

So yes, buying new hardware is sometimes a case of hoping that someone will make a patch for it, and you're better off looking at hardware that's at least a year old and double-checking that someone coded up support for it before you buy. But I prefer that over the driver dance any day.

There's also a giant, green elephant in the room: Nvidia. I don't use an Nvidia GPU, but I have heard that those who do sometimes need to grab official drivers from outside the kernel, meaning they don't have the same pleasure of having everything bundled straight into the kernel. Fortunately, it's more an exception than the rule, but it's still worth me mentioning, as it highlights how hardware developers do sometimes need to play nicely for everything to work properly.

Hardware support is still one of Linux's biggest problems, and it may never change

Companies need to get on board

34
By  João Carrasqueira

Linux doesn't have it all, but I love what it does have

The Linux way of things is by no means perfect, but it's by far my fave. Dodging the driver hunt, having all my USB peripherals work on any distro with zero additional work, and getting longer support for my devices than a manufacturer would give me all outweigh the negatives in my mind.

item.title: I finally found a free open-source tool that can replace PowerPoint, Canva, and Claude Design for presentations
item.itunes:title: I finally found a free open-source tool that can replace PowerPoint, Canva, and Claude Design for presentations
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Presentation software is one of those tools almost everyone ends up needing, whether that's for a class project or something you agreed to months ago and completely forgot about. But the catch is that the popular options usually tend to hold back their best features for paying users. PowerPoint comes bundled with Microsoft 365 and the Personal plan is now $100 a year. Canva now keeps most of its templates and AI allowance behind the Pro subscription. And even though Claude Design is available to free users now, it's heavily capped.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Free alternatives have been around forever, but many of them feel like a downgrade the minute you try to open a .pptx file that someone else sent you. Fonts get swapped out for something else and the animations get glitchy or go completely missing, so you just end up fixing slides instead of presenting them.

DeckCraft attempts to fix all of this, and it comes pretty close to being a free stand-in for all three of them. It's one of the still-growing collection of open-source apps from the ArtCraft suite, which was built by developer Brandon Thomas with the help of Claude Opus 5.5. I've tested a bunch of tools from this collection this past month and must say this feels like "vibe-coding" done right. And DeckCraft is no exception.

A PowerPoint alternative that actually opens your files

Opening someone else's deck is usually where free apps lose me

Opening a real PowerPoint file is the first thing I check with any free alternative, since that's usually where the formatting starts to slip. DeckCraft opens and saves .pptx natively, and it can import older .ppt files too, although those get saved under a new name instead of being overwritten.

The ArtCraft team calls it a clean-room rebuild of PowerPoint, which means they recreated how PowerPoint works without using any of Microsoft's code or assets, so the layout and user flow feel very familiar. Slide masters and 11 standard layouts are supported, so changing fonts or spacing on a master updates the placeholder text boxes in layouts that inherit from it.

Presenting is also pretty comprehensive especially considering the app is technically still in alpha. Morph is included, which is the transition that animates objects from one slide into the next, and presenter view comes with rehearse timings for practicing against the clock. Exports go beyond plain PDF, with notes pages and handouts that keep their text selectable, and you can save slides out as PNG or JPEG images or turn the deck into an animated GIF.

The developers rate it at about 55% ready to replacing PowerPoint for real work. So I'd still keep important work saved elsewhere, to be completely honest.

I tried replacing Photoshop, Lightroom, and Acrobat with free vibe-coded alternatives, and they're surprisingly good

Got to give credit where credit's due

11
By  Mahnoor Faisal

The design tools that rival Canva

There isn't a template library, but there's a lot more control

Canva's biggest draw has always been templates and it has over 1.6 million on the free plan alone. But this is one area where DeckCraft doesn't compete. You get a handful of original starter decks and eight themes, but the starters are color schemes with placeholder text rather than designed templates, so there are no accent bands or picture treatments. I only use them as a base to drop my own content into.

However, the template library isn't Canva's only sell, it also has pretty advanced manual design control, and this is where DeckCraft starts to compete. It has over 150 preset shapes with adjust handles, and you can merge shapes together (union, intersect, subtract, and a couple of others) to build custom graphics. Connectors stay glued to shapes when you move them which saves me a lot of effort fiddling with the diagram slides. Effects also go deeper than Canva. There's gradient, pattern fill, shadows, and reflections, and I can adjust each one down to the pixel.

DeckCraft had a WordArt feature then renamed it to Decorative Text, and it comes with six preset styles you can drop onto a slide and then restyle with the same fill and effect options as any other shape. For data-heavy slides, there are native charts and styled tables, along with a basic version of SmartArt (called Diagram here) for things like process flows.

I replaced the Adobe suite with a free open source alternative that Claude can control directly

Artcraft clones Adobe's apps for free, and Claude can run them for you.

9
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Where the AI comes in

Bringing your own AI instead of Claude Design

Claude Design takes a prompt and builds an entire deck for you, while DeckCraft has no AI built in at all. What DeckCraft does instead is treat every button in its interface as a command, and those commands are available through an MCP server, which is the standard way AI assistants connect to outside apps. That means Claude or a local model can open a deck and build slides by running the same actions you'd click on yourself.

There's no button in the app to connect an assistant, so you need to use the terminal and run a command to start DeckCraft's MCP server before your AI can see it - you'll find it in DeckCraft's README on GitHub. You can confine an agent to specific folders, so it won't be able to go through the rest of your files.

Cost is probably the biggest difference here. Claude Design is included with every Claude plan, including Free now, and its usage counts toward your plan's limits. If you're not subscribed, you know how quickly the cap hits, and if you are, you know how easy it is to dig into Extra Usage. But DeckCraft doesn't run a model at all, so what you pay depends on whichever AI you connect to it, and with a local model that could be nothing. It also works in .pptx from the start, whereas Claude Design builds decks in HTML and converts them when you export.

An open-source Adobe suite built with AI is almost ready to replace the real thing

ArtCraft has seriously impressed me

6
By  Ty Sherback

It's still in alpha but already doing a lot

Canva is often recommended as a more user-friendly and design-forward PowerPoint alternative, but DeckCraft gets closer to replacing PowerPoint than Canva does. For anyone who builds slides from scratch, the editing tools already cover a lot, and the AI side works for those who are comfortable in the terminal. DeckCraft really does cover all the bases.

item.title: My TV shows my own photo library when nobody's watching, and it never phones home
item.itunes:title: My TV shows my own photo library when nobody's watching, and it never phones home
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Many modern smart TV ambient modes lock photos/slideshows behind cloud ecosystems, compress image quality, or inject sponsored content and telemetry alongside personal photos. I don't want to have a persistent internet connection just to display a basic screensaver.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

My solution was to host a personal photo library locally via Immich on an existing NAS, then pull those photos onto the TV over the local area network via a dedicated client app. By feeding my pictures to my TV directly from a self-hosted local server, my display becomes a zero-telemetry, zero-subscription digital gallery that no longer serves me ads or recommendations.

The software stack is simple

But it varies based on the TV you have

My first thought when I wanted to display my photo library on my TV was to use a built-in USB slideshow, but I quickly noticed it had a lot of friction. Despite the simple method of plugging a USB flash drive directly into your TV, it's impractical for daily use, as it requires me to manually unmount it, copy new photos over, and it lacks dynamic album creation. Depending on your TV, it can also suffer from clunky, dated built-in media players.

Instead, I decided to use Immich, an open-source self-hosted photo and video backup solution. It runs via a Docker Compose stack on minimal hardware — I host it on a two-bay consumer NAS. Once it's set up, it automatically organizes uploads from your phone over local Wi-Fi.

Once my Immich setup was sorted, the next thing I needed to do was set up the TV client. This will depend on what TV and setup you have. For Google TV, you can use a dedicated third-party open-source client like Immich TV that connects directly to a local IP address rather than requiring a domain name, reverse proxy, or SSL certificate. If you have an Apple TV, you can use Immich Frame or a local SMB share piped into the native Apple TV Photos/Screen Saver app via a local Mac/NAS share (if you're hoping to avoid third-party apps entirely).

I have an LG TV where there's no official Immich app in the LG Content Store itself, so I had to install a community-built client by installing the LG Developer Mode app from the store and then installing the IPK with the WebOS Dev Manager on my PC. I went with Immich-Lite, a lightweight alternative designed specifically for older LG TVs running WebOS 3 and 4.

Why I stopped buying smart TVs, and what I bought instead

Remember when smart features worked for us, instead of against us?

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

I blocked my TV from the internet altogether

I got fed up with the ads

While I didn't have to, I decided to take this a step further and sever my TV's internet connection altogether. When a smart TV remains connected to the internet, you get background DNS queries to manufacturer tracking domains as well as firmware updates that can re-enable ACR. The ultimate issue for me is the constant UI slowdowns caused by ad carousels loading on the home screen.

One solution is to never connect your TV's built-in smart OS to Wi-Fi or Ethernet and instead plug in an external streaming stick. However, this does come with the issue of your TV not being connected to your local network either, which means this Immich trick won't work. So I decided to block WAN access at the router level, so my TV stayed connected to the LAN. I assigned a static IP to my TV in my router's admin panel. I then applied a WAN block. This might sometimes fall under parental control settings or firewall rules. Target your TV's specific IP address to drop all outbound traffic to the internet while permitting local subnet traffic.

This way, your TV or streaming box retains full high-bandwidth access to your local Immich server over Wi-Fi or Ethernet while any attempt to reach external cloud servers, ad networks, or update servers will fail.

Lastly, it was time to set it as a screensaver

I wanted my photos to appear when I walked away

The last issue I needed to overcome was manually setting up the Immich app whenever I wanted the screensaver active. But there is a way to trigger this logic automatically so that your photo gallery appears seamlessly when left idle rather than requiring manual app launches. Depending on your TV, you can configure the Immich app as the system's default ambient mode service:

For Google TV, go to Settings, then System Settings, select your Ambient Mode, and set the timer to trigger after however many minutes of inactivity works for you. On Apple TV, you can point the native Aerial/Photo screensaver settings to the local shared album and set Start After to the specified amount of time.

I set up a dedicated TV display album in Immich, and added new photos from my phone, which automatically updated what appeared on the screen within seconds over LAN. No USB drives or cloud uploads required. I also enabled slow pan/zoom and hid any static UI overlays in the client app settings to prevent static element retention or burn-in on my TV screen.

I finally found an open-source tool that casts web video to my TV without hijacking my PC screen

My PC finally learned to share, but not its screens

2
By  Samarveer Singh

There's minimal maintenance

And it's all free

Photos taken on my phone now appear on my living room TV automatically over local Wi-Fi, without any cloud compression, and my screen never displays ads or prompts for privacy policy re-acceptance.

Once the initial 20-minute Docker and router setup was complete, the ongoing system requires zero subscription, zero cloud storage fees, and minimal maintenance. I don't want to deal with data collection and ad impressions, so I want to treat my TV strictly as a local display panel and keep personal media on my own hardware.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Wi-Fi dead zones are a common headache in larger homes, and running Ethernet cable through walls isn't an option for everyone. That's where the TP-Link AV2000 Powerline Ethernet Adapter comes in, since it sends your network over the electrical wiring you already have. Amazon is running it as a Black Friday deal, knocking $14 off its usual $89.99 price to $75.89, its lowest price since December 2025.

The TP-Link AV2000 Powerline Adapter transforms the electrical circuits in your house into a hardwired data line for high-speed Internet.

A handy fix for spotty connectivity

Wired internet without the cable clutter

Powerline adapters carry your network over your home's electrical wiring, so they suit situations where you want a wired connection but can't run Ethernet cable between rooms. Instead of a wireless signal that has to get through walls and furniture, the data travels through the outlets already in your home. It's a practical choice for finished walls or rentals where drilling isn't realistic, and that's the idea behind this TP-Link adapter.

The listing is for the TL-PA9020P KIT, a starter kit with two adapters, each with two Gigabit Ethernet ports. TP-Link rates its powerline physical-layer speed at up to 2,000 Mbps.

A wired connection is a good fit for stationary devices in a room with weak Wi-Fi, such as a desktop, a game console, or a smart TV. Wi-Fi can be affected by interference, while a physical connection can be steadier, which may mean fewer lag spikes and less buffering during games and 4K streams. A console or work desktop in a back bedroom is the classic example.

Keep in mind that powerline performance can vary from home to home, since it depends on the wiring behind your walls. Any top speed on the product page is a manufacturer's figure, not a guarantee of what you'll see in your own house, so set your expectations accordingly.

TP-Link is a well-known name in home networking, but without a review directly from us, the Amazon listing details and customer ratings are worth a read before you commit. If your router already sits close to the room you're trying to cover, or Wi-Fi works fine there, you probably don't need one. This is for the rooms where your wireless signal gives up.

For anyone who needs a stable wired connection in a room Wi-Fi can't reach, $75.89 on Amazon is a fair price for a TP-Link Powerline Adapter. It's not a replacement for good Wi-Fi everywhere, but for one stubborn room, it's a straightforward fix. Grab the TP-Link AV2000 Powerline Ethernet Adapter while you can.

item.title: My coding agents kept forgetting what I told them until I gave every project one shared instructions file
item.itunes:title: My coding agents kept forgetting what I told them until I gave every project one shared instructions file
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Repeating the same instructions to every coding agent I've ever used got old very quickly. I'd tell a model to run `npm run lint` before marking a task complete, then have to remind it the next day to keep doing that. This became an even bigger burden when my set of established coding rules and conventions grew into an unwieldy list that I was pasting across every session.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The answer was an AGENTS.md file at the root of every project. It's a simple Markdown file that all agents read when they start up, so they always begin a task with the same level of initial context. I dumped everything in there that I could possibly need an agent to know before getting started, and now I'm able to switch between Claude Code and Codex without needing to repeat anything between the two agents.

AI coding agents made me a better programmer, but only after I stopped letting them write the code

Don't let coding agents completely steer your ship.

3
By  Anurag Singh

Every agent gets the same memo

One file contains all instructions

Every time I fire up a new session with a coding agent, it starts with a fresh context window. Since every project is unique and each developer has their own approach to how things get done, it takes some time for an agent to get familiar with the project and its conventions. From working with Claude Code, I know that it takes its own notes, but those are saved to a temporary filesystem by default and stay on one machine.

I've invested a lot of time into making a custom set of rules for each project, making the instructions almost as important as the code itself. That's why I like to commit the AGENTS.md file right alongside the source code. If your project already has a CLAUDE.md file, you will need to add an import inside of it, which is just `@AGENTS.md` on one line. Otherwise, Claude will find the former file and stop looking for more.

The AGENTS.md file is supported by Codex, Cursor, Claude Code, and most of the other big names, so it's the perfect place to store instructions that you don't want to tie to a specific company. That's the opposite of a file like CLAUDE.md, which is the recommended place to put Claude-specific instructions. You could also use a README, but I'd argue that's more for human eyes and should house things like installation instructions, while also warranting differently written language.

Record everything that's not obvious

And the stuff you're sick of repeating

At first, I was documenting everything I could inside of AGENTS.md. I think that instinct stemmed from years of writing README files for people who wouldn't bother looking at the code. But AI agents will be perusing the codebase anyway, so there's no reason to be redundant by specifying a bunch of facts that can easily be derived from looking through the source files. Jamming more information than necessary into AGENTS.md just puts it more at risk of something falling out of date, and makes the file more difficult to maintain.

It's worth it to take some extra time to think about how your wording will be interpreted by AI. For example, "test your changes" is pretty ambiguous. Instead, I'll tell models to run `npm test` after it's finished with changes, and to fix any errors that arise before committing. For big changes to the UI, I tell the model to spin up a test environment and use Playwright (a browser for testing) to make sure everything looks right. Being vague will get unpredictable results, so I list specifics instead.

The file is never really "complete" though. Projects change over time, so I find myself updating the instructions every once in a while. I added another line to the file that says, "If changes you make render a set of instructions in AGENTS.md irrelevant or obsolete, notify the user about it and recommend how it should be updated." That has helped me shift some of the upkeep of the file to the AI models themselves.

This won't magically fix problems

It just makes prompting AI a bit smoother

Throwing all your instructions into this file won't actually make the agent any more powerful. The only thing it really does is save me some keystrokes and keep me from sounding like a broken record. The same amount of work still gets done as before, but now the whole process feels a little smoother than it was.

I didn't create the file with the goal to extract more power or efficiency out of whichever model was helping me code that day. It was mainly for my own sanity, because there were a pile of project-specific conventions and quirks that I'd end up repeating every time I opened a new prompt. The biggest sections of my AGENTS.md are "need-to-knows," "project layout," "database info," and "auth and users," all of which contain only the essential rules every agent will need in order to get started.

Type it once and never say it again

Here's an easy rule of thumb: if you've typed the same instruction across two different agent windows, then it's worth giving that rule its own bullet point in AGENTS.md. Starting with the most common annoyances first is easy, and you'll get a few lines just from that. It'll grow quickly from there, but it feels so good to dive straight into a project without bringing the agent up to speed first.

item.title: I gave each Docker container its own Tailscale address, and stopped exposing ports on my home server
item.itunes:title: I gave each Docker container its own Tailscale address, and stopped exposing ports on my home server
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Docker is a fantastic tool to isolate your self-hosted tools from each other and maintain a robust, fail-proof home server. The traditional way to access the web portal of any container is via its published port. Each port number is a direct gateway to access the portal, but it gets tedious after a point. You have to be careful with the port number assignment and also need to remember them. Exposing ports is something that we rarely pay attention to, and it slowly becomes complex.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Tailscale is already a staple tool on my home servers, and if you want to ditch the port mappings, you can use Tailscale Sidecars. These are individual containers that work alongside each service and give them a unique Tailscale identity. It’s even possible to enable HTTPS support for each container. But there’s a tool that makes it much easier.

Tailscale Sidecar is useful

But there's still a lot of legwork

When I first learned about Tailscale’s sidecar feature, I was sure that it would solve the external port publishing problems. The feature simplifies the idea and reduces the need to publish ports on my home server. Tailscale Sidecar gives each container a unique network identity, hostname, and IP address. So, there would be no need to publish the external port for the application on the host. I can use the Tailscale IP as a replacement for port publishing.

It sounds easy until you start creating sidecars for each self-hosted tool deployed as a Docker container. Now, you need to authenticate each Sidecar, specify the internal port for each self-hosted tool, and configure Docker networking. The result is worth the effort because you can now access the web portals of the tools with simple URLs and no dependency on port publishing.

I replaced my reverse proxy with Tailscale Serve for private services, and I'm not going back

Private services routed through a mesh identity layer, instantaneous TLS, and far fewer firewall headaches await.

17
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

But doesn't it seem like too much work? On a low-end SBC like a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, you might need to do this for 3–4 lightweight containers. On more powerful servers with dozens or more containers, it becomes frustrating. I haven't even included the additional time needed to configure HTTPS support for each one. So, is Sidecar worth the effort? Well, no. It's a perfect tool, but you can improve this whole process with a tool like TSDProxy.

Shrinking everything to just one container

TSDProxy acts as a central manager

The main selling point of Tailscale is a private, secure network where all the connected devices can communicate with each other. You can access your home servers even when you are outside the local network with Tailscale. But system-wide Tailscale deployment and then subsequent Tailscale Serve mappings for each container become confusing.

It doesn’t assign a new identity to each Docker container, so managing access to individual containers can become cumbersome. To sum up my problems, I’m frustrated with individual sidecar deployments, authentication, and the lack of automatic HTTPS support. TSDProxy addresses all three pain points and works as a separate container.

When you deploy the TSDProxy container, you effectively get rid of individual sidecar deployments, and it can still manage separate Tailscale proxy identities. Your container list remains succinct. After a one-time setup and authentication, all the containers configured to use TSDProxy become accessible on your Tailnet.

Docker isn't the hard part of self-hosting, and the part that is gets skipped by almost everyone

This admin is fundamental.

5
By  Jasmine Mannan

A typical setup of TSDProxy involves generating a Tailscale authentication key. You need to visit the Settings page in the Tailscale dashboard and then generate a new key. Name it, keep the “Reusable” option checked, and then copy the generated key somewhere safe. Thereafter, you can create all the necessary folders for the tool with the following commands:

mkdir -p /opt/tsdproxy-stack/config
mkdir -p /opt/tsdproxy-stack/data
mkdir -p /opt/tsdproxy-stack/authkey

Now, open the authkey file, paste the key, and save the file. You can also restrict direct access to this file.

nano /opt/tsdproxy-stack/authkey/tsdproxy-authkey

Next, you need to create the configuration and compose files, and then deploy the TSDProxy container on your server. Most of the work is done, and now you only need to tweak the config files of each container to use the TSDProxy network.

You also don’t need to publish a new port for access like before. However, you need to redeploy each container so TSDProxy can begin automatic detection and configure its Tailscale access.

Easily add new containers to the Tailnet

No more individual sidecar deployments

In the previous section, all the existing containers now use the TSDProxy connection to get new Tailscale identities. But if I wanted to add a new container and also assign it a new Tailscale identity. I would only need to modify the config files of each container to use the proxy connection and recreate them with Docker Compose.

labels:
  tsdproxy.enable: "true"
  tsdproxy.name: "vaultwarden"
  tsdproxy.port.1: "443/https:80/http"

These three lines tell the Vaultwarden container to use the TSDProxy connection, assign a friendly name to it, and use the internal port 443 for HTTPS and 80 for HTTP. It’s a small effort compared to creating new sidecars for each container. One more thing that it achieved without configuration is HTTPS support. I didn’t need to configure HTTPS certificates individually because TSDProxy enables it by default for each configured container using Tailnet addresses.

Smarter container networking

TSDProxy simplifies remote access and HTTPS support for your Docker containers. You switch from individual sidecars to a single container to manage Tailscale identities for the rest of the Docker containers. No more manual sidecar configurations, individual authentications, or Tailscale Serve commands.

Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS

Tailscale is a tool that allows you to create specific network connections so you can remotely access resources within a private network.

item.title: I haven't bought a new drive for my home lab in years, and my old ones keep proving me right
item.itunes:title: I haven't bought a new drive for my home lab in years, and my old ones keep proving me right
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When upgrading a PC, server, network-attached storage (NAS), or simply replacing a drive, the old hard disk drives (HDDs) and solid-state drives (SSDs) were either discarded or thrown into a storage box somewhere. I was the same. If I was upgrading storage somewhere, the old drive would be extracted and binned or locked away somewhere. That was until the price of drives and memory started to skyrocket in recent years. Now, I always reuse everything from a system, including old drives.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Every drive can have a new lease of life

Even if it's a 250GB SSD

Credit: 

The home lab doesn't demand much. I have a single small-form-factor (SFF) system running as a network video recorder (NVR). It has 16 GB of DDR4 RAM, an Intel Core i5-7400 CPU, and a small SSD to run Proxmox and a few containers. That SSD has been in use for almost a decade at this point, and it refuses to give up, which is fantastic for me since I sourced this platform as a barebones box from a classified site. I popped in the old SSD, and we were good to go.

The same goes for the primary node in the home lab, running Proxmox on a Minisforum U850. It has a capable mobile Intel chip with 16 GB of RAM and another small 250 GB SSD. Now, using such a small storage drive isn't the best idea when it comes to running a few heavy VMs and LXCs, but it does the job until I eventually hit the ceiling and need to migrate everything to another drive. I'm almost there at this point, with 33% and 92% of local pools in use.

What these SSDs provide is the means to set up and launch these home lab systems without forking out on new hardware. A 250 GB SSD will set you back $40 with a Black Friday deal. That's $40 for a SATA SSD, working out to be around $0.16 per GB, which is an incredible amount to pay for local storage. To put it into perspective, I view $0.02 to $0.06 as the sweet spot for spending per GB for storing lots of data. It's why the cost of everything is increasing.

But it's also a great opportunity to make better use of older parts, especially if they're doing nothing but collecting dust. I wouldn't dream of buying a 250GB SATA SSD for my gaming PC today, but I'd happily install another one in a Proxmox node if I had one lying around.

I ditched HDDs for an all-SSD NAS — here’s why I went back

The trade-offs I didn’t expect

3
By  Karandeep Singh

Old drives are still more than enough

You don't need PCIe 5.0 SSDs inside every device

We've managed to launch some incredible tech over recent years. The speeds that modern PCIe SSDs can hit are nothing short of incredible, but it's also largely pointless for the home lab. Granted, SATA interfaces top out at around 550 MB/s, but that's actually more than enough for most local network setups. Unless you're using 2.5Gb networking (or faster), these drives will easily saturate your network with file transfers.

And that's for hard drives, which are notably slower than SATA SSDs; the latter being the better fit for storage drives inside home lab servers. The system running my NVR doesn't require a ridiculously fast NVMe SSD to boot Proxmox or launch Frigate. Likewise, a server handling a few lightweight Docker containers or LXCs doesn't necessarily need thousands of megabytes per second of sequential transfer performance.

An old SATA SSD capable of hitting around 500 MB/s can still be plenty fast for these tasks. The more important benefit of using an SSD over a mechanical drive for an operating system is its ability to quickly access numerous small files without waiting for a physical read/write head to move across spinning platters. That's something even an older SATA SSD can do remarkably well compared to an HDD. And there's a better chance you have SATA drives to spare than NVMe.

But really, how often will your storage be used to its maximum throughput? Many of the services I run barely touch the storage drive during normal operation, outside of isolated spikes. Applications can make extensive use of system memory, and while there will be some disk activity for databases, logs, and other persistent data, I'm unlikely to notice the difference between an older SATA SSD and a modern NVMe drive for many of my lighter workloads.

Used enterprise hard drives are the last real storage deal, and I trust them more than new ones

The pre-owned enterprise storage market is alive and well

1
By  Ty Sherback

Used mechanical drives are gold for data

Unleash a more affordable NAS with plenty of space

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

You've likely seen SSD caching and even all-SSD NAS coming to market, but I don't see myself retiring mechanical drives from the home lab NAS anytime soon. They're fantastic for storing a lot of data, often surpassing the available capacities of consumer-grade SSDs. But they're also incredibly reliable. I'm still spinning platters that are almost a decade old inside my NAS. And modern NAS platforms will work with different drive capacities.

Smaller HDDs that I would no longer consider installing inside a desktop PC can also be useful. A spare 2TB drive may not seem particularly impressive nowadays, especially with the size of modern PC games, but that's a considerable amount of capacity for storing backups of individual virtual machines, configuration files, and other home lab data. Take my security NVR server as an example with its 2TB mechanical drive.

My NVR uses an SSD to run Proxmox and Frigate, while a secondary mechanical drive handles the recordings. This separates the operating system and application workloads from the constant stream of video data and avoids using valuable SSD capacity for footage that will likely be automatically deleted a few days later. Writing a metric ton of data to SSDs also isn't going to make them last, which is where an old HDD can step in.

Stop choosing sides – the smartest NAS setup uses both SSDs and HDDs

Even if you're a hardcore data hoarder, you should opt for a hybrid NAS configuration

1
By  Ayush Pande

Get creative, but don't blindly trust drives

One important thing I bear in mind when looking through old drives I have, or when sourcing used and refurbished units, is to check SMART reports and run some real-world tests. I also employ a 3-2-1 backup strategy with multiple local copies of everything valuable, so should the worst happen to our NAS, everything is backed up somewhere for quick retrieval. Next time you come across an old drive, consider what you could use it for.

item.itunes:summary:
My productivity setup had become unnecessarily complicated. I relied on Todoist to manage my daily tasks, Toggl to track how much time I spent on individual projects, and a separate Pomodoro timer to maintain focus throughout the day.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That’s when I came across Super Productivity, a free, open-source app that combines task management, time tracking, and focus sessions into a single workspace.

7 productivity suites you've probably overlooked (and might suit you better)

Stop using the same old tools

By  Parth Shah

Super Productivity caught my attention
